title: Infra GPU fleet, cloud accounts & IaC CI/CD playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates operational guidance for the infra engineering team that runs the GPU fleet and related cloud account, networking, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD pipelines. It is intended for engineers onboarding to infra, SREs supporting capacity, and on-call responders for provisioning and incidents.

Sections in this document:
1) Capacity targets and SLOs
2) Cloud accounts & networking (bootstrapping and tagging)
3) Terraform/IaC module design and patterns
4) CI/CD pipeline for infra modules and GPU images
5) Day-2 runbooks (scaling, incident response, rollback)
6) Ownership and contact matrix
7) Examples and snippets (CLI, Terraform, YAML)

1) Capacity targets and SLOs

Short summary:
- Objective: keep service-level token latency targets met for production inference routing and ensure cost-efficient GPU utilization.
- Fleet SLOs (applies to prod GPU pools):
  - Median inference tail latency (p95) for 1k-token requests: < 1200ms (per model route)
  - Node-level GPU utilization: target 70% (good range 60%-80%)
  - Cluster-level free capacity for burst: >= 10% of committed capacity
  - Pod/container eviction due to OOM: < 0.5% over 30 days

Capacity planning guidance:
- Maintain two capacity buffers: a reactive buffer (10% of active capacity) and a proactive buffer for region failover (15% of active capacity).
- Scale-up trigger (automated): average cluster GPU utilization > 78% for 30m and queue length > 50 pending requests across all routes.
- Scale-down trigger (automated): average cluster GPU utilization < 55% for 60m and no sustained queueing.
- Manual capacity add: submit a capacity request ticket with KPI: expected peak RPS, model footprints (vram/slot), projection period, and requested start date. Owners will triage within 24 hours.

Sizing checklist for new model onboarding:
- Provide model TFLOPs, VRAM requirement per shard, expected concurrency per replica, and average tokens per request.
- Use the sizing worksheet template (link: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026#sizing) to compute replicas and GPU counts.

2) Cloud accounts & networking

Account structure and guardrails:
- We use a multi-account pattern: org-root -> prod, staging, dev, shared-services. Each account has standardized IAM roles, guardrails in SCPs, and audit logging.
- Account bootstrap sequence (new region / new account):
  1. Create account via internal account-creation service (owner: cloud-accounts team).
  2. Apply baseline Terraform state (networking VPC, core subnets, NAT/IGW, route tables).
  3. Attach centralized logging and security stacks (CloudTrail/Logging -> centralized S3 with encryption + access audit role).
  4. Create role mappings for infra CI/CD and SRE oncall roles.
  5. Register account in fleet-ops inventory (infra-catalog).

Networking rules:
- GPU pools must be provisioned in private subnets with controlled egress via NAT + egress gateway for model downloads.
- Internal service CIDR allocation: 10.32.<region-id>.0/20 for GPU pools; add route entries for cross-account peering to the shared services account.
- Security groups: minimal open ports. Allow only management plane (SSH from bastion via SSM), node-exporter metrics (TCP/9100) and runtime ports required by the serving runtime (config per model-service).

Tagging and naming policy (must be enforced in IaC):
- Tags required: project, owner, environment, cost-center, created_by, terraform_version. Example: {project: gpu-fleet, owner: infra-ops, environment: prod, cost-center: platform}

3) Terraform/IaC module design and patterns

Repository layout (recommended):
- repo: infra-modules (monorepo) with directories: modules/, envs/prod/, envs/staging/, envs/dev/, tools/ci-pipelines/.
- Module granularity: small, composable modules. Examples: vpc, subnet, gpu-instance-group, iam-roles, s3-backend, kms-keys.

State management and locking:
- Remote state backend: S3 bucket with server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) + DynamoDB for state locking. Backend configuration example provided in snippets.
- Workspaces: use one workspace per environment (prod, staging, dev). Avoid long-lived feature workspaces for IaC changes.

Versioning and compatibility:
- Each module must include a changelog, semantic versioning, and a pinned provider version. Major version bumps should include an ADR linking to the change impact.

Module acceptance criteria (PR checklist):
- Module has input/output docs in README.md.
- Unit tests with terratest or terraform-compliance where applicable.
- Example usage in envs/ with planable defaults.
- Security review (static checks) green: checkov, tfsec.

Backend example (S3 + DynamoDB):
- backend.tf snippet (example):
  terraform {
    backend "s3" {
      bucket = "redwood-infra-tfstate-prod"
      key    = "envs/prod/gpu-fleet/terraform.tfstate"
      region = "us-west-2"
      dynamodb_table = "redwood-tf-locks"
      encrypt = true
    }
  }

Secrets and bootstrap credentials:
- Use the bootstrap role (assume-role) for the CI runner to assume per-account deploy role. Never embed long-lived keys in repo.

4) CI/CD pipeline for infra modules and GPU images

Pipeline stages (for infra modules):
1. Lint: terraform fmt, validate, checkov, tfsec
2. Unit tests: terratest / module unit checks
3. Plan: terraform plan with workspace=branch-preview -> stored artifact
4. Plan review: announce plan in PR with diff and impact
5. Approvals: protected envs (prod) require two approvers including an oncall engineer and a security reviewer
6. Apply: run in a short-lived runner that assumes deploy role and runs terraform apply with --auto-approve behind approval gate

CI runner and permissions:
- Runners run in the shared-services account with an ephemeral IAM role that can assume per-account deploy role (sts:AssumeRole). The deploy role is constrained by IAM condition on source pipeline arn.

GPU image build pipeline (Bento/Docker):
- Stages: build -> smoke-test (run sample model) -> image-scan (clair/trivy) -> push to ECR -> register AMI (if using images for on-prem) -> notify.
- Image tagging scheme: project/gpu-serving:<semver>-sha256(<short>) e.g., gpu-serving:2026.02.10-1a2b3c

Rollback strategy for IaC changes:
1. If terraform apply introduces regression, revert the module version in envs/ and re-run CI to apply the previous stable plan.
2. If state drift occurs: open a drift ticket, isolate resource, and use an emergency plan with targeted resource replacement (terraform apply -target=...).
3. For destructive changes, pipeline must block unless release manager approves after a post-plan mitigation doc.

5) Day-2 runbooks

Runbook: add capacity (automated + manual)
- Automated scale (HPA/cluster-autoscaler style for GPU groups): when triggered, CI will create additional instance groups according to the scaling policy.
- Manual add (24-48 hour lead preferred):
  1. Open a capacity request ticket with numbers (region, desired gpu-type, expected start/end).
  2. Infra-capacity owner reviews and confirms quota availability and networking.
  3. Create a capitalizable change in envs/prod/ with new instance group module & run CI plan.
  4. Run plan in staging; if successful, apply to prod behind approval gates.
  5. Validate: check model routing metrics, per-node utilization, and end-to-end latency.

Runbook: degraded model serving due to capacity shortage
1. Pager fires for run queue length or p95 latency breach.
2. Oncall: assess the alert dashboard (gpu-pool-overview, routing-queue, model-latency).
3. If shortage is due to temporary burst: shift routing to non-peak region using routing policy OR increase ephemeral burst pool (preconfigured via autoscale action).
4. If shortage persists: run the emergency scale plan (apply targeted instance-group).
5. Post-incident: update capacity projections and run a root-cause analysis.

Runbook: failed Terraform apply (lock/stage drift)
1. Check DynamoDB lock for stale locks. If lock is stale for > 15 minutes and owner unresponsive, follow the lock release policy: contact owner -> if unreachable, escalate to infra oncall to remove lock after verifying no active CI jobs.
2. Inspect plan artifacts for unauthorized destructive ops. If detected, cancel apply and restore previous state (revert PR).

7) Examples and snippets

Terraform backend snippet:
```
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "redwood-infra-tfstate-prod"
    key            = "envs/prod/gpu-fleet/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-west-2"
    dynamodb_table = "redwood-tf-locks"
    encrypt        = true
  }
}
```

Assume-role example (AWS CLI):
```
aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/infra-deploy-prod --role-session-name ci-deploy
```

Quick terraform workflow (local dev):
1. terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-infra-tfstate-dev"
2. terraform workspace new feature/your-branch || terraform workspace select feature/your-branch
3. terraform plan -var-file=envs/dev/terraform.tfvars

CI job sample (GitHub Actions YAML excerpt):
```
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2
      - name: Terraform fmt + validate
        run: terraform fmt -check && terraform validate
      - name: Terraform plan
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.out
```

Monitoring and dashboards
- Key dashboards: gpu-pool-overview, gpu-node-health, model-routing-latency, terraform-plan-impact. Set alerts:
  - GPU utilization high: warn at 75%; urgent at 85% sustained 15m
  - Plan failure rate > 3% in 24h -> notify infra-iac
  - DynamoDB lock age > 15m -> page oncall
